item.title: South Carolina First, Iowa Out: Inside the New 2028 Democratic Primary Calendar Shaking Up the Party
item.body:
## A New Order for Choosing the Next Democratic Nominee

The Democratic National Committee has formally signed off on the presidential nominating calendar for 2028, and the headline change is hard to miss: South Carolina, not Iowa, will be the first state to vote. The decision, finalized by the full DNC after months of work by its Rules and Bylaws Committee, closes the book on Iowa's decades-long run as the traditional opening contest of presidential primary season and cements a realignment that began quietly in the 2024 cycle.

For a party that spent nearly half a century sending White House hopefuls first to Iowa's town halls and church basements, the shift is more than a scheduling footnote. It is a statement about which voters the party believes should have the first say in picking its next standard-bearer.

## What the 2028 Calendar Looks Like

According to the calendar approved by the DNC, six states will make up the party's official early window, all voting before Super Tuesday on March 7, 2028:

- **South Carolina** — January 22
- **Nevada** — February 1
- **New Hampshire** — February 8
- **New Mexico** — February 15
- **Michigan** — February 22
- **Virginia** — February 29

That is two more states than were in the early window for 2024, after the Rules and Bylaws Committee voted over the summer to expand the group from four or five states to six, adding New Mexico and Virginia to the mix. Every region of the country recognized by the DNC is represented, a structural requirement the committee set out when it began the selection process in late 2025.

## Why Iowa Lost Its First-in-the-Nation Status

Iowa's removal from the early lineup did not happen overnight. The state's Democratic caucuses had already been pushed out of the top spot for 2024, largely because of the chaotic 2020 caucus, when a reporting app malfunction delayed final results for days and undermined confidence in the process. That episode, combined with long-standing criticism that caucuses draw far fewer and less representative voters than primaries, gave party leaders the opening to rethink the order.

South Carolina's rise reflects a different argument: that the party's early states should better reflect the coalition that actually elects Democrats, including the large Black electorate that has proven decisive in past primaries. Nevada's continued early placement is tied to similar reasoning about racial and economic diversity, along with its strong union presence.

## New Hampshire's Complicated Position

New Hampshire remains in the early window, but not first, which keeps alive a long-running tension between the DNC and the state. New Hampshire law requires its secretary of state to schedule the nation's first primary, a statute the state has enforced for a century. That legal mandate led New Hampshire to hold an unsanctioned primary ahead of the party's approved calendar in 2024, prompting the DNC to strip the state of delegates as a penalty. How that friction resolves for 2028 — whether New Hampshire falls in line with its February 8 slot or again moves earlier on its own — is one of the more closely watched subplots of the new schedule.

## Why the Calendar Matters Beyond the Dates

Primary calendars are rarely just logistics. Going first confers outsized media attention, fundraising momentum and a psychological edge for candidates who can claim an early win. States near the back of the line, by contrast, often see contenders drop out before voters even head to the polls. That dynamic is why fights over calendar order have flared in both parties for decades, and why South Carolina Democrats, who helped revive Joe Biden's 2020 campaign after early losses in Iowa and New Hampshire, have pushed hard to keep their state at the front.

Party officials involved in the process have framed the changes as an effort to modernize a nominating system that many voters and strategists viewed as outdated, while critics argue the reshuffling still leaves plenty of room for future disputes, particularly if states continue to jockey for position or ignore the party's approved order.

## What Comes Next

With the calendar locked in more than a year before voting begins, prospective 2028 candidates now have a clearer map for building early campaign infrastructure, hiring staff and courting voters in the six early states. Expect increased political activity in South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia well ahead of the formal campaign season, as would-be nominees try to establish themselves in the states that will set the tone for the race to come.
